scenes.title: What is AI?
scenes.description: Maya sees speech become written words, a picture recognised and notes become a draft. These demonstrations introduce AI before returning to Maya at home.
lines: AI is short for artificial intelligence.
It’s a broad name for computer systems that can recognise patterns, make predictions, work through problems or create things like text and pictures.
For example, some tools can turn spoken words into writing.
Others can help you put together a first draft.
Meet Maya.
She works at a community centre and keeps hearing people talk about AI.
Today, a few familiar situations will help her understand what it can do and where she still needs to check its work.

scenes.title: Does everything automatic use AI?
scenes.description: In her kitchen, a timer follows a set countdown. Maya then dictates a reminder and sees spoken words become writing. A simple diagram distinguishes human-supplied knowledge from learning patterns.
lines: Maya’s kitchen timer rings.
She set the time herself, and the timer follows that instruction.
It can do this without AI.
Next, she speaks a reminder into her phone.
Her words appear as text.
Some tools use AI to recognise speech.
Both tasks happen automatically, but that doesn’t mean they work in the same way.
AI can be built in different ways, too.
Some systems use knowledge and rules supplied by people.
Others learn patterns from examples.
Simply following a rule doesn’t automatically make a program AI.
Let’s look at learning from examples.

scenes.title: How can examples help?
scenes.description: Labelled cat and dog pictures move through a training diagram. Separate unfamiliar test pictures receive predictions, including a wrong prediction for a partly hidden animal.
lines: Imagine a system being trained to recognise cats and dogs in pictures.
During training, it receives pictures with labels saying which animal they contain.
It uses those examples to learn patterns.
We’re showing a small selection here to explain the idea.
Afterwards, we try pictures it hasn’t trained on.
Can it use those patterns to recognise the animal?
Sometimes it gets the answer right.
Sometimes it makes a mistake.
An unfamiliar picture or a partly hidden animal can be difficult.
Learning patterns from data is called machine learning.
It’s one way to build AI.
The examples used for training, and how well the system handles new situations, both matter.

scenes.title: Can AI help Maya get started?
scenes.description: At the community centre, Maya enters a fictional request for a Tuesday team meeting in Room Two. A private contacts document stays outside the tool. The tool generates an invitation draft.
lines: At work, Maya needs to invite her colleagues to a team meeting.
She knows what she wants to say, but getting started is taking a while.
She opens a tool her workplace allows and types: ‘Draft a friendly invitation to our team meeting on Tuesday in Room Two.’
She keeps private information about colleagues out of the request.
The tool produces a draft.
This is an example of generative AI, which creates content such as text, pictures or audio.
Maya now has something to work with.
Before she uses it, she needs to read it.

scenes.title: Where did that time come from?
scenes.description: The draft claims nine oclock without a supplied time. Maya compares it with the actual calendar entry at ten thirty, then corrects the draft.
lines: Hang on.
The invitation says the meeting starts at nine.
Maya didn’t give the tool a time, and she hasn’t connected it to the team calendar.
She checks the calendar herself.
The meeting starts at half past ten.
The draft sounds confident, but that detail is wrong.
Generative AI can produce information that sounds convincing without being true.
Maya corrects the time using the meeting record.
Asking the tool whether it is sure would not replace that check.
A useful draft still needs someone to check the facts.

scenes.title: What should Maya remember?
scenes.description: Maya reviews the corrected invitation, chooses to send it and reflects on how AI can help. A final invitation asks learners to explain AI in their own words.
lines: Maya reads the invitation again.
The details are right, it says what she means, and she chooses to send it.
AI helped her get started.
Maya checked the result and made the decision.
AI can help us recognise patterns, make predictions and create content.
Some AI learns from examples, and some uses knowledge and rules.
Not every automatic feature is AI.
Before using a result, ask: does this fit my task, and which details need checking?
Keep private information protected.
For decisions that could seriously affect someone’s life, involve an appropriately qualified person.
Now, tell me, how would you explain AI to someone who has never used it?
